title: Acharei Mot: not at all times (Leviticus 16:2)
hookLine: even the high priest may enter the holiest place only once a year

lines: THE FIRST RULE IS A NO.
A ROOM HE CAN'T WALK INTO.
cards: We live in an age of always. Stores open all night. Messages at three in the morning.
Every show, every song, every person a tap away, any hour. The idea that something should be off limits most of the time can feel almost foreign.
The first instruction Moses receives for Yom Kippur isn't about what Aaron should do. It's about what he shouldn't.
The high priest, who wears the golden plate engraved holy to the LORD, is told there's a room he may not simply walk into.

teach.h: NOT AT ALL TIMES, BEHIND THE VEIL.
teach.b: The verse, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: tell Aaron "that he come not at all times into the holy place within the veil." Behind that curtain is the holy of holies, the ark and its cover.
The chapter goes on to describe one day, the tenth of the seventh month, when the high priest goes in, with incense and blood, on behalf of everyone. Only that day.
Some readers draw a lesson: the closer you are to the center, the more the limits matter. There's care inside the limit, too.

teach.h: A SHORT PRAYER, NOT TO FRIGHTEN.
teach.b: The Mishnah describes the high priest coming out of the holy of holies and saying a short prayer in the outer room. Short, it says, so as not to frighten the people waiting outside.
The limit isn't coldness; everyone outside is holding their breath for him.

teach.h: A WEEK FROM CAMP TO SANCTUARY.
teach.b: Look back at the week. Metzora opened with the priest going out of the camp. Then cedar and hyssop, a bird set free, a house emptied before the verdict, and a person walked home step by step.
Acharei Mot began with grief before atonement.
And now: not at all times. Jewish life is full of these boundaries. Shabbat closes the week's work at sundown.
Some things are kept for one night a year. Some find the limit is what keeps a thing precious. A door you can open any time can stop being a door.

how: On Yom Kippur, the Musaf service in traditional synagogues retells the high priest's service in the holy of holies, called the Avodah, and Shabbat rest is another limit that sets time apart.

games.why: the Mishnah says he prayed a short prayer, so as not to frighten Israel. care inside the limit.

practice: Think of something that would mean more if it weren't available all the time: your phone at the dinner table, work email after dark, a conversation you keep reopening.
Choose one limit you could keep, just for this evening, and picture the door closing gently, and what might have room to grow on the other side of it.
